title: The First Explanation Is Often the Easiest One, Not the Strongest One

Don’t Ask the Signal to Explain More Than It Can Bania Putri Product Strategy Evidence Decision Making Research Strategy The First Explanation Is Often the Easiest One, Not the Strongest One Bania Putri 6 min read · Oct 8, 2026 -- Listen Share Three cases on competing mechanisms, different interventions, and what evidence needs to establish before explanation becomes decision. Founder Notes 01 | STRIVE Evidence Systems One pattern keeps appearing across my work: the same observable signal can often be produced by very different underlying mechanisms. A customer doesn’t use a product. Is the underlying need weak, or is adoption too difficult? A customer purchases but doesn’t continue. Was acquisition successful while persistent value remained weak? A product performs below expectation. Is demand weaker than expected, is the solution poorly matched to the need, or is delivery limiting the result? In each case, what we observe is real. What produced it is not yet established. The easiest response is often to attach an explanation immediately: “They aren’t interested.” “They don’t understand.” “The product isn’t valuable enough.” “The market isn’t ready.” Sometimes that explanation is correct, but the observation itself usually doesn’t prove it. I’ve become increasingly interested in the distance between what we observe and what we think caused it. That distance matters because different mechanisms can require very different interventions. Case 1 — Low Usage: Weak Need or Adoption Friction? Suppose a digital product has strong initial sign-ups, but usage falls quickly. One explanation is that users don’t need the product enough. If that’s true, adding more onboarding, reminders or promotional incentives may accomplish very little. The underlying need may simply be too weak to sustain usage, and the company might need to reconsider its target segment, problem relevance or value proposition. But another explanation is possible: the need is real, but using the product requires too much effort. Customers may genuinely want the outcome but encounter complicated onboarding, workflow disruption, confusing interfaces or other adoption friction. Now the appropriate intervention changes. The company may not need a new market. It may instead need to remove the barriers preventing an existing need from becoming regular usage. The observed signal is identical: low usage. But weak underlying need would suggest reconsidering demand, segment or value proposition, while adoption friction would suggest improving the path between need and usage. Misdiagnose the mechanism, and the company can spend years improving usability for a market that never needed the product strongly enough. Or it can abandon a valuable market because it mistook difficulty of adoption for absence of demand. The observation tells us something important about behavior. It does not, by itself, establish which mechanism produced that behavior. Case 2 — Customers Explore but Don’t Choose: Communication or Relative Advantage? Suppose customers repeatedly explore a product but don’t buy it. It is tempting to conclude that they don’t understand the product. So the company explains more. Demonstrations improve, educational content expands, messaging becomes more detailed, and sales teams receive better material and scripts. All of these interventions may genuinely improve communication. But what if customers understand the product perfectly well and simply don’t see enough advantage over what they already use? Then additional explanation does not solve the underlying problem. The issue may instead be differentiation, economics, switching costs, use-case relevance or the actual value offered relative to alternatives. Again, the same observable outcome can be consistent with different mechanisms, and those mechanisms direct the organization toward different interventions. One diagnosis encourages the company to improve communication, while the other encourages it to reconsider the offer itself. This distinction becomes more consequential over time because organizations can become increasingly sophisticated at improving something that was never the main constraint. Marketing can improve, sales scripts can improve, product demonstrations can improve, and teams can become faster and more capable at explaining the product. Yet customers may continue making exactly the same choice because the underlying relative advantage remains insufficient. This creates a distinction I increasingly find important: improvement in an intervention does not necessarily validate the diagnosis that produced the intervention. An organization can become better at an activity without becoming better at solving the underlying problem. Case 3 — Strong Acquisition, Weak Continuation: What Did the Campaign Actually Establish? Suppose a campaign produces a large increase in new customers. Acquisition looks successful, and the immediate interpretation might be that demand is growing. The company increases acquisition spending, expands the campaign, adds capacity or uses acquisition numbers as evidence that the market is responding. But several weeks later, many of those customers disappear. Now the original signal requires more careful interpretation. The campaign established that customers could be persuaded to acquire. It did not necessarily establish that the product generated sufficient value for them to continue.
